mainTopic: The future redemption will overshadow, but not erase, יציאת מצרים. The rule of עיקר and טפל, and a new opening about the name change of אברם to אברהם.
overview: The עמוד opens by finishing a ברייתא. In the future, יציאת מצרים will not be forgotten, but it will become טפל to the final redemption, just as ישראל became יעקב's main name while יעקב stayed as a secondary name. A משל about a wolf, a lion and a snake shows that newer troubles push older ones aside. The גמרא then explains why אברם became אברהם and why שרי became שרה. בר קפרא and רבי אליעזר rule that one may not call אברהם 'אברם'. The גמרא defends that rule against challenges from שרה, from יעקב, and from a פסוק in נחמיה. פרק מאימתי ends, and פרק היה קורא opens with a משנה about reading שמע with כוונה, when one may interrupt שמע to greet someone, and why its paragraphs come in their order. The גמרא shows that the משנה does not prove מצוות צריכות כוונה. It then analyzes the מחלוקת between רבי and the חכמים over saying שמע in any language, including the source each side uses for every rule. Finally, a ברייתא begins on how much of שמע needs כוונה: רבי אליעזר limits it to the first part, and רבי עקיבא begins to reply, with his פסוק coming on the next עמוד.

steps.title: יעקב's name stays, but becomes secondary
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains that 'no longer will your name be יעקב' does not mean the name יעקב is erased. It means ישראל becomes the main name and יעקב becomes secondary.
steps.simpleTranslation: It does not mean that the name 'יעקב' is uprooted from its place. Rather, 'ישראל' is the main name and 'יעקב' is secondary to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its comparison. Just as יעקב's old name was kept as a secondary name, יציאת מצרים will be kept as a secondary memory.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'your name shall no longer be called יעקב', yet the Torah keeps calling him יעקב afterward. So 'no longer' cannot mean 'never again'. It means 'no longer as the main name'. The same reading applies to the פסוק about not mentioning יציאת מצרים in the future: it will still be mentioned, but as טפל.

keyTerms.meaning: that it will be uprooted (completely removed)
from its place
the main, primary thing
secondary, subordinate

steps.confusionAlert: This is not saying the name יעקב (or the memory of יציאת מצרים) disappears. Both remain; only their rank changes from main to secondary.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of עיקר and טפל is how the ברייתא reconciles 'no longer will they say' with the ongoing duty to remember יציאת מצרים.

phrases.english: Not that the name 'Jacob' will be uprooted from its place,
but rather 'Israel' is the primary name,
and 'Jacob' is secondary to it.
phrases.notes: The Torah still uses 'Jacob' after the name change, which proves the old name was not erased.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא's comparison, begun on the previous עמוד, between the name change of יעקב and the future status of יציאת מצרים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'No longer' in a פסוק can mean 'no longer as the main thing', not total removal. ישראל is עיקר and יעקב is טפל.

steps.title: A verse in Isaiah supports the same idea
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings a פסוק from ישעיה: 'Do not remember the former things, do not ponder the old ones'. It reads 'former things' as שעבוד מלכיות and 'old ones' as יציאת מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it says: 'Do not remember the former things, and do not ponder the old things.' 'Do not remember the former things' refers to שעבוד מלכיות. 'Do not ponder the old things' refers to יציאת מצרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a פסוק as further support. It shows that in the future, great earlier events will fade in importance compared to the new redemption.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses two words for the past: ראשונות (former) and קדמוניות (very old). The ברייתא matches the more recent one, ראשונות, to שעבוד מלכיות, and the older one, קדמוניות, to יציאת מצרים. Both will be outshone by the final redemption, which fits the idea of becoming טפל.

keyTerms.meaning: and so it says (introduces a supporting פסוק)
former things
things of old, very ancient events
subjugation to the (foreign) kingdoms, i.e., exile
the Exodus from Egypt

phrases.english: And so it says:
'Do not remember the former things,
and do not ponder the things of old' (Isaiah 43:18).

phrases.aramaic: אַל תִּזְכְּרוּ רִאשֹׁנוֹת״ — זֶה שִׁעְבּוּד מַלְכֻיוֹת,
phrases.english: 'Do not remember the former things' refers to the subjugation to the kingdoms,
'and do not ponder the things of old' refers to the Exodus from Egypt.
phrases.notes: יציאת מצרים is 'older' than the גלות, so it matches the word 'things of old'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second פסוק to support the idea from step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That in the future, earlier redemptions will be overshadowed by the final redemption.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיה 43:18, 'אל תזכרו ראשונות וקדמוניות אל תתבוננו'.

steps.title: רב יוסף: the 'new thing' is מלחמת גוג ומגוג
steps.stepSummary: On the next פסוק, 'Behold I am doing a new thing, now it will sprout', רב יוסף teaches that the new thing is מלחמת גוג ומגוג.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it will spring forth.' רב יוסף taught: this is מלחמת גוג ומגוג.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues with the next פסוק in ישעיה. רב יוסף identifies the 'new thing' that will make people forget the earlier events.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 said not to dwell on the old events. This פסוק says why: something new and greater is coming. רב יוסף explains that this new event is the great final war of גוג ומגוג.

keyTerms.meaning: a new thing
taught (a ברייתא)
the war of Gog and Magog, the great war at the end of days

phrases.english: 'Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it will spring forth' (Isaiah 43:19):
Rav Yosef taught:
This is the war of Gog and Magog.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the next פסוק, which names the event that will overshadow the earlier ones.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'new thing' in ישעיה 43:19 is מלחמת גוג ומגוג.

steps.title: The parable of the wolf, the lion and the snake
steps.stepSummary: A traveler escapes a wolf and tells that story. Then he escapes a lion and tells that story. Then he escapes a snake, forgets both earlier stories, and tells only the snake story.
steps.simpleTranslation: A parable: to what is this similar? To a person walking on the road. A wolf attacked him and he was saved, and he kept telling the story of the wolf. A lion attacked him and he was saved, and he kept telling the story of the lion. A snake attacked him and he was saved; he forgot the story of both, and he kept telling the story of the snake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משל, a story-picture, to make the idea easy to feel. This step is the story itself; its lesson comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each danger is worse than the last, so each rescue is a bigger miracle. A person naturally talks about the most recent and greatest rescue. The older stories are not false; they simply fade from his telling.

keyTerms.meaning: a parable, a comparison story
attacked him, encountered him
and he was saved
kept on telling
the story, the incident

phrases.english: A parable: to what is this similar?
To a person who was walking on the road,
and a wolf attacked him, and he was saved from it,
and he kept telling the story of the wolf.
A lion attacked him, and he was saved from it,
and he kept telling the story of the lion.
A snake attacked him, and he was saved from it,
he forgot the story of both of them,
phrases.notes: Both = the wolf and the lion.

phrases.english: and he kept telling the story of the snake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates, through a parable, why a newer, greater event (step 3) pushes aside older ones (step 2).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person tells the story of his latest and greatest rescue, and the earlier ones fade.

steps.title: The lesson: newer troubles make the older ones forgotten
steps.stepSummary: The נמשל: the same is true of ישראל. Later troubles, and the rescues from them, cause the earlier ones to be forgotten.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too with ישראל: the later troubles cause the earlier ones to be forgotten.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the parable to כלל ישראל and closes this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wolf, lion and snake match the rising troubles of ישראל across history. The rescue from the latest and greatest trouble will become the main story, so יציאת מצרים will become טפל. This ties the whole section back to step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: so too, likewise
later troubles
cause to be forgotten

steps.whatToRemember: In the future, יציאת מצרים will still be remembered, but as טפל. The final redemption will become the עיקר, just as ישראל became the main name and יעקב the secondary one.

phrases.english: So too with Israel:
the later troubles cause the earlier ones to be forgotten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the parable of step 4 to ישראל.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Later troubles and redemptions overshadow earlier ones, so the final redemption will make יציאת מצרים secondary but not erased.

steps.title: New topic: אברם is אברהם
steps.stepSummary: Having discussed יעקב's name change, the גמרא now quotes a פסוק about אברם becoming אברהם, opening a parallel discussion.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'אברם is אברהם.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא quotes a פסוק to open a new discussion about the name change of אברם to אברהם, which will be explained next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic of name changes led from יעקב and ישראל to אברהם. The פסוק 'אברם הוא אברהם' (דברי הימים א 1:27) is quoted here only as a heading. Its meaning is explained in the coming lines.

keyTerms.meaning: The original name of אברהם
His changed name

phrases.english: 'Abram is Abraham' (I Chronicles 1:27).
phrases.notes: A heading verse; the explanation follows in the next part of the גמרא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The discussion of יעקב's name change prompts a related discussion of אברם's name change.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduces the פסוק about אברם becoming אברהם as the basis for the next discussion.

steps.title: Why אברם became אברהם
steps.stepSummary: The name change shows that אברהם grew from a father to ארם into a father to the whole world.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first he became a father to ארם, and in the end he became a father to the entire world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the meaning of the פסוק quoted in step 6 about אברם becoming אברהם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The old name אברם is read as 'אב ארם', a father (a leader) of ארם only. The new name אברהם is read as 'אב המון גוים', a father of many nations. So the name change marks a change in how far his influence reaches.

keyTerms.meaning: At first, initially
In the end, ultimately
A father (leader) to ארם, the source of the name אברם
The entire world

phrases.english: Initially he became a father to Aram,
phrases.notes: אברם = אב + ארם

phrases.english: and ultimately he became a father
phrases.notes: The added letter ה points to 'אב המון', father of a multitude

phrases.english: to the entire world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the meaning of the אברם/אברהם פסוק quoted in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name change shows that אברהם went from local leadership over ארם to being a father to the whole world.

steps.title: The parallel name change of שרי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the parallel case: שרי, who is the same person as שרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'שרי is שרה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It brings up שרי's name change so it can explain it the same way it explained אברהם's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words mean that שרי and שרה are one person, so the same kind of change applies to her. The explanation itself comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: 'My princess', her original name
'Princess' with no 'my', her new name

phrases.english: "Sarai is Sarah."
phrases.notes: Introduces the parallel to אברם/אברהם

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the name-change discussion from אברהם to שרה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שרי and שרה are the same person, and her name change parallels אברהם's.

steps.title: Why שרי became שרה
steps.stepSummary: שרי was a princess only to her own nation. As שרה she became a princess to the whole world.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first she became 'שרי' to her nation, and in the end she became 'שרה' to the entire world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains שרי's name change using the same pattern it used for אברהם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'שרי' means 'my princess', which is limited and belongs to her own people. 'שרה' means simply 'princess', with no limit, so it applies to everyone. Like אברהם, her importance grew from local to worldwide.

keyTerms.meaning: To her nation, her own people
She became

steps.whatToRemember: Both name changes follow one pattern: from local importance (ארם / her own nation) to worldwide importance (the whole world).

phrases.english: Initially she became Sarai (a princess) to her nation,
phrases.notes: The suffix 'י' = 'my', limiting her status

phrases.english: and ultimately she became Sarah
phrases.notes: No limiting suffix, so she is a princess in general

phrases.english: to the entire world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the quote from step 8, copying the pattern of step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שרה's name change marks her move from princess of her own nation to princess of the whole world.

steps.title: Calling אברהם by his old name breaks a positive commandment
steps.stepSummary: בר קפרא teaches that anyone who calls אברהם 'אברם' violates an עשה, based on 'your name will be אברהם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: בר קפרא taught: Anyone who calls אברהם 'אברם' violates a positive commandment, as it says: 'And your name will be אברהם.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from the meaning of the name to a practical rule: you may not call אברהם by his old name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בר קפרא reads the words 'your name will be אברהם' as a command, not only a prediction. Since it is phrased as something you must do, ignoring it is a violation of an עשה.

keyTerms.meaning: Taught (introduces a ברייתא-level teaching)
A sage from the transition period between the תנאים and the אמוראים
Violates a positive commandment
One who calls

phrases.english: Bar Kappara taught:
Anyone who calls Abraham "Abram" —
transgresses a positive commandment.
as it is stated: "And your name will be Abraham."
phrases.notes: בראשית יז:ה, read as a positive command

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the aggadic meaning of the name change to a practical rule about using the name.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Calling אברהם 'אברם' violates an עשה derived from 'וְהָיָה שִׁמְךָ אַבְרָהָם'.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: it breaks a negative commandment
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר says calling אברהם 'אברם' violates a לאו, based on 'your name shall no longer be called אברם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: He violates a negative commandment, as it says: 'And your name shall no longer be called אברם.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר agrees that using the old name is forbidden, but he says the violation is a negative commandment (לאו).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sages draw from the same פסוק. רבי אליעזר focuses on the earlier words 'ולא יקרא', which are phrased as a prohibition. That makes the violation a לאו instead of an עשה.

keyTerms.meaning: Violates a negative commandment (a prohibition)
'And it shall no longer be called', the prohibition wording
As it is stated (introduces a פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: Everyone agrees one may not call אברהם 'אברם'. בר קפרא says it violates an עשה ('וְהָיָה שִׁמְךָ'). רבי אליעזר says it violates a לאו ('וְלֹא יִקָּרֵא עוֹד').
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a dispute about whether it is forbidden. Both agree it is forbidden. They only disagree about which kind of commandment is broken, and each one points to a different phrase in the same פסוק.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says:
he transgresses a negative commandment,
as it is stated: "And shall no longer be called
phrases.notes: The negative wording of the פסוק

phrases.english: your name Abram."
phrases.notes: בראשית יז:ה

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a competing view on what kind of violation is involved in בר קפרא's case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Calling אברהם 'אברם' violates a לאו derived from 'וְלֹא יִקָּרֵא עוֹד אֶת שִׁמְךָ אַבְרָם'.

steps.title: Does calling שרה 'שרי' also break a מצוה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule from the last two steps. If calling אברהם 'אברם' breaks a מצוה, then calling שרה 'שרי' should break one too.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if that is true, then someone who calls שרה 'שרי', does he also break a מצוה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the rule of בר קפרא and רבי אליעזר one step further and finds a problem. שרה's name was also changed, so the same rule should apply to her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 8-9 showed that שרי became שרה, just as אברם became אברהם. If the name change for אברהם creates a מצוה, the same should be true for שרה. But nobody treats calling her 'שרי' as a sin, so the rule looks too broad.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But now, according to this...' A formula that takes a rule and shows a surprising result that seems to follow from it.
One who calls (someone by a name).
'So too?' Here it asks: does the same rule apply in this case as well?

phrases.english: But if so, from now on
phrases.notes: This signals a challenge: if your rule is true, then look what follows.

phrases.english: one who calls Sarah 'Sarai'
phrases.notes: Using her old name.

phrases.english: does he also (transgress)?
phrases.notes: Asked as a challenge, not just out of curiosity.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה הַקּוֹרֵא לְשָׂרָה ״שָׂרַי״ הָכִי נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule from steps 10-11 to the parallel case of שרה and finds a problem.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that calling someone by a name that was changed breaks an עשה or a לאו.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שרה's name was changed just like אברהם's. So the rule should forbid calling her 'שרי', yet that seems wrong.

steps.title: The command about שרה's name was given only to אברהם
steps.stepSummary: The verse about שרה's name was spoken only to אברהם. So it is not a general מצוה for everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is different: הקב"ה said to אברהם, 'Your wife שרי, you shall not call her name שרי, because שרה is her name.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It points out that the verse about שרה was a private instruction given only to אברהם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With אברהם, the verse says in general terms, 'your name shall no longer be called אברם.' That applies to everyone. With שרה, the verse is addressed to אברהם alone: 'you (אברהם) shall not call her שרי.' So other people are not commanded about her name.

keyTerms.meaning: There, meaning in that other case.
The Holy One, Blessed be He.
'You (singular) shall not call.' It is addressed to one person.

steps.confusionAlert: The answer does not say שרה's name change was less real. It only says that the command was given to אברהם alone, not to everyone.

phrases.english: There, the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Abraham:
phrases.notes: The key point: the speech was directed at אברהם only.

phrases.english: 'Sarai your wife,'

steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases based on who the verse is speaking to.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every name change from a verse creates a מצוה for everyone.
steps.terutzMaskana: שרה's verse was a command to אברהם alone. Only אברהם's own name change was stated as a general command.

steps.title: Does calling יעקב 'יעקב' also break a מצוה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a second challenge. יעקב's name was changed to ישראל in general terms, so calling him 'יעקב' should be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if that is true, then someone who calls יעקב 'יעקב', does he also break a מצוה?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a harder case. The answer about שרה does not work for יעקב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: About יעקב, the verse says 'Your name shall no longer be called יעקב, but ישראל' (בראשית 32:29). Like the verse about אברהם, this is said in general terms, not as a private command to someone else. So the rule should forbid the name 'יעקב', yet everyone uses it.

keyTerms.meaning: The אב whose name was changed to יִשְׂרָאֵל.
'Your name shall no longer be called יעקב' (בראשית 32:29). This is the פסוק behind the challenge, though the גמרא does not quote it here.

phrases.english: But if so, from now on
phrases.notes: The same challenge formula is used again.

phrases.english: one who calls Jacob 'Jacob'
does he also (transgress)?!
phrases.notes: Said with surprise, because everyone calls him יעקב.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה הַקּוֹרֵא לְיַעֲקֹב ״יַעֲקֹב״ הָכִי נָמֵי

steps.kashyaTarget: The rule of בר קפרא and רבי אליעזר about name changes.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: יעקב's name change was stated in general terms, just like אברהם's. So the rule should forbid calling him 'יעקב'.

steps.title: The תורה itself calls him 'יעקב' again
steps.stepSummary: יעקב is different, because later on the verse itself goes back to calling him 'יעקב'.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because the verse itself went back to the old name, as it is written: 'And אלקים said to ישראל in the visions of the night, and He said: יעקב, יעקב.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge about יעקב‎. ה׳ Himself later calls him 'יעקב', so the old name was not fully cancelled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once ה׳ uses the name 'יעקב' after the change (בראשית 46:2), that name is clearly still allowed. With אברהם, the תורה never goes back to 'אברם'. So the rule of בר קפרא and רבי אליעזר stands for אברהם alone.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is different.' This introduces a distinction between cases.
The verse went back and returned to it, meaning it used the old name again.
As it is written.
Visions of the night.

steps.whatToRemember: It is forbidden to call אברהם 'אברם'. שרה is different, because her command was spoken only to אברהם. יעקב is different too, because the תורה itself calls him 'יעקב' again later.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the גמרא reads verses closely. It asks who is being spoken to, and whether the תורה ever uses the old name again.

phrases.english: It is different there,
because the verse went back and returned it (the old name),
as it is written:
'And God said to Israel
phrases.notes: בראשית 46:2. This comes after the name change.

phrases.english: in the visions of the night,
and He said: Jacob, Jacob.'
phrases.notes: ה׳ Himself uses the old name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about יעקב.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case with a later verse that uses the old name again.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: יעקב's name change cancels the name 'יעקב' completely, just like with אברהם.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since ה׳ Himself later calls him 'יעקב', that name is still permitted. Only 'אברם' is forbidden.

steps.title: A פסוק in נחמיה calls אברהם 'אברם'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר אבין (or רבי יוסי בר זבידא) challenges the rule against calling אברהם 'אברם' from a verse in נחמיה that calls him 'אברם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר אבין, and some say רבי יוסי בר זבידא, raised an objection: the פסוק says, 'You are ה׳, God, Who chose אברם!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third challenge to the rule of בר קפרא and רבי אליעזר that one may not call אברהם 'אברם'. A verse in נחמיה, written long after the name change, still calls him 'אברם'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If saying 'אברם' breaks a לאו, a later verse should not use that name. Yet נחמיה 9:7 says 'Who chose אברם'. So either the rule is wrong, or this verse needs an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection, usually from a source
And some say (another version of who said it)
You chose
אברהם's original name, before ה׳ changed it

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin raised an objection,
and some say it was Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is unsure which of two names to attribute the objection to.

phrases.english: 'You are ה׳, God,
phrases.notes: Nehemiah 9:7

phrases.english: Who chose Avram'!
phrases.notes: The verse uses the old name 'אברם'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the challenges from שרה and יעקב were answered, a new challenge comes from a verse in נביאים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule of בר קפרא (an עשה) and רבי אליעזר (a לאו) that calling אברהם 'אברם' is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A verse written after the name change still calls him 'אברם', which suggests the name is not forbidden.

steps.title: The prophet was retelling what happened at first
steps.stepSummary: The verse is not calling him 'אברם' now. The נביא is praising ה׳ by retelling history, including how things were before the name change.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, the prophet is listing the praises of the Merciful One, describing what was at the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. נחמיה uses 'אברם' only because he is telling the story of what ה׳ did back when that was his name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The לאו forbids calling אברהם by his old name as his current name. Describing history ('ה׳ chose אברם') is a different thing, because it reports the past. In fact, the same verse goes on to say 'and You made his name אברהם', so the name change itself is part of the praise.

keyTerms.meaning: There (in that verse)
Prophet
Arranges / lists His praises
The Merciful One (ה׳)
At the beginning, originally

steps.whatToRemember: The לאו is against calling אברהם 'אברם' as his name today. Retelling the history from before the name change is allowed.

phrases.english: He said to him:
There, it is the prophet
who is listing the praises of the Merciful One,
describing what was at the beginning.
phrases.notes: This means the time before ה׳ changed his name to אברהם.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection from נחמיה in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Context of the verse: it is historical retelling, not current naming
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any use of the name 'אברם' after the change, even in a verse, would contradict the לאו.
steps.terutzMaskana: Using 'אברם' to describe events from before the name change is not a violation. The rule of בר קפרא and רבי אליעזר stands.

steps.title: הדרן — Closing פרק מאימתי
steps.stepSummary: The first chapter of ברכות, מאימתי, ends with the traditional closing formula.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'From what time'.
steps.whatsHappening: This is not an argument. It is the formula that marks the end of the first chapter, פרק מאימתי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Learners say הדרן at the end of each chapter to show they intend to come back and review it. The name מאימתי comes from the first word of the chapter's opening משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you (said at the end of a chapter)
'From what time', the name of the first chapter of ברכות

phrases.english: We will return to you, 'From what time'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the whole chapter after the last discussion ends in step 17.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: פרק מאימתי, about the times of קריאת שמע and related topics, is complete.

steps.title: Reading the שמע passage when its time comes counts if one had כוונה
steps.stepSummary: The new chapter's משנה rules that someone reading the Torah passage of שמע when the time for קריאת שמע arrives fulfills his obligation if he had כוונה.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone was reading in the Torah, and the time for reciting שמע arrived, if he directed his heart, he has fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter, פרק היה קורא, opens with a משנה. It describes a person who is reading the parsha of שמע as Torah study just when the time to say קריאת שמע arrives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words he says are the same either way. What decides the matter is whether he 'directed his heart'. The משנה does not spell out what that כוונה is. It could be intent to fulfill the מצוה, or only intent to actually read the words. The גמרא debates this in steps 26–29.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
He was reading (also the name of the new chapter)
The time for reciting קריאת שמע
He directed his heart (had כוונה)
He fulfilled his obligation

steps.confusionAlert: 'כִּוֵּון לִבּוֹ' here can be read in two ways. It may mean he intended to fulfill the מצוה. It may instead mean he paid attention to the words, as opposed to just checking the text. The גמרא will discuss this, which links to the question of whether מצוות צריכות כוונה. Do not assume the meaning is settled yet.
steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה opens the major topic of כוונה in מצוות, which is a foundational question across all of halacha.

phrases.english: MISHNA: If one was reading in the Torah
phrases.notes: He was reading the Torah section of שמע as study.

phrases.english: and the time for reciting שמע arrived,
if he directed his heart, he has fulfilled his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new chapter after the הדרן in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Reading the parsha of שמע at its proper time fulfills the obligation only if the reader has כוונה.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: when you may greet during שמע
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר rules that בין הפרקים one may greet and answer מפני הכבוד, and באמצע one may greet and answer מפני היראה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Between the sections, a person may greet someone out of respect, and may answer a greeting. In the middle of a section, he may greet someone out of fear, and may answer. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives רבי מאיר's rule for when you may stop קריאת שמע to say 'שלום' to someone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two levels of interruption. At a break between sections (בין הפרקים), the bar is lower: you may stop even just to show respect (כבוד) to an important person. In the middle of a section (באמצע), the bar is higher: you may stop only out of fear (יראה), for example if the person could harm you. For רבי מאיר, starting a greeting and answering one follow the same rule at each level.

keyTerms.meaning: Between the sections, meaning the breaks between the paragraphs and ברכות of שמע
In the middle of a section
He greets first, literally 'asks' after the other person's welfare (שְׁאִילַת שָׁלוֹם)
He responds to someone else's greeting
Out of respect, such as for a father, teacher, or important person
Out of fear, for someone who might harm you if ignored

steps.confusionAlert: In this משנה, 'שואל' does not mean asking a question. It means initiating a greeting of שלום.

phrases.english: At the breaks between sections, one may greet out of respect, and may respond.
phrases.notes: The easier case: a break point in שמע, so respect alone is enough.

phrases.english: And in the middle, one may greet out of fear, and may respond,
phrases.notes: The harder case: only fear justifies interrupting mid-section.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
phrases.notes: Tells us this is one side of a מחלוקת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה of היה קורא. After the basic rule of reading שמע with כוונה, it now addresses interruptions during שמע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בין הפרקים: greet and answer מפני הכבוד. באמצע: greet and answer מפני היראה.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: answering a greeting is easier than starting one
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rules that באמצע one may greet out of fear but answer out of respect, and בין הפרקים one may greet out of respect and answer anyone at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: In the middle, one may greet out of fear and answer out of respect. Between the sections, one may greet out of respect and answer 'שלום' to every person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה argues with רבי מאיר. He treats answering a greeting as more lenient than starting one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה shifts the answering rule down one level at each point. In the middle, starting a greeting still needs fear, but answering needs only respect. Between sections, starting a greeting needs respect, but you may answer anyone, even someone you owe no special honor. The reasoning is that ignoring someone who greeted you is more insulting than not greeting them first.

keyTerms.meaning: Returns a greeting of peace
To every person, even someone with no special status

steps.whyThisMatters: The pattern of answering being more lenient than initiating is the core of the מחלוקת. It is a useful key for remembering the whole משנה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
phrases.notes: Introduces the opposing view.

phrases.english: In the middle, one may greet out of fear
phrases.notes: Same as רבי מאיר for starting a greeting.

phrases.english: and may respond out of respect.
phrases.notes: More lenient than רבי מאיר: answering needs only respect.

phrases.english: And at the breaks between sections, one may greet out of respect
phrases.notes: Same as רבי מאיר for starting a greeting.

phrases.english: and may respond with a greeting to any person.
phrases.notes: Most lenient: you may answer anyone.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בָּאֶמְצַע, שׁוֹאֵל מִפְּנֵי הַיִּרְאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי מאיר's ruling in step 20 by separating starting a greeting from answering one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: באמצע: greet מפני היראה, answer מפני הכבוד. בין הפרקים: greet מפני הכבוד, answer anyone.

steps.title: What counts as בין הפרקים
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists the five break points in קריאת שמע and its ברכות that count as בין הפרקים.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the breaks between the sections: between the first ברכה and the second, between the second ברכה and שמע, between שמע and והיה אם שמוע, between והיה אם שמוע and ויאמר, and between ויאמר and אמת ויציב.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה defines its own term. It tells us exactly which spots in שמע are 'between the sections'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since both opinions depend on whether you are בין הפרקים or באמצע, we need to know where the breaks are. There are five: two among the ברכות before שמע, two among the three paragraphs of שמע, and one between the last paragraph (ויאמר) and the ברכה after שמע (אמת ויציב). Anywhere else counts as באמצע.

keyTerms.meaning: The first ברכה before שמע (יוֹצֵר אוֹר)
The second ברכה before שמע (אַהֲבָה רַבָּה or אַהֲבַת עוֹלָם)
The second paragraph of שמע
The third paragraph of שמע, the section about ציצית
The ברכה said right after שמע in the morning

phrases.english: These are the breaks between the sections:
phrases.notes: Introduces a definition list.

phrases.english: between the first blessing and the second,
phrases.notes: Break 1

phrases.english: between the second and 'Shema',
phrases.notes: Break 2

phrases.english: between 'Shema' and 'VeHaya im Shamoa',
phrases.notes: Break 3

phrases.english: between 'VeHaya im Shamoa' and 'VaYomer',
phrases.notes: Break 4

phrases.english: between 'VaYomer' and 'Emet VeYatziv'.
phrases.notes: Break 5. רבי יהודה will dispute this one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the term בין הפרקים used by both רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are five break points in שמע and its ברכות that count as בין הפרקים.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: no interrupting between ויאמר and אמת ויציב
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rules that the gap between ויאמר and אמת ויציב is not a break at all, so one may not interrupt there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: Between ויאמר and אמת ויציב, one may not interrupt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the last item on the list. He says the spot between ויאמר and אמת ויציב is not a break point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion counts this spot as a regular break, so the lenient rules of בין הפרקים apply there. רבי יהודה says this spot is not a break at all, so those lenient rules do not apply, and ויאמר should be joined straight to אמת ויציב. The common explanation is that the last words of שמע, 'ה׳ אֱלֹהֵיכֶם', are meant to join directly with the first word of the ברכה, 'אֱמֶת'.

keyTerms.meaning: He may not interrupt
An interruption

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה has two separate מחלוקות. The first is how lenient to be about greetings. רבי יהודה is more lenient about answering a greeting than רבי מאיר. The second is whether the gap between ויאמר and אמת ויציב is a break. רבי יהודה says it is not, so no interruption is allowed there.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the custom of saying 'ה׳ אֱלֹהֵיכֶם אֱמֶת' together without pausing at the end of שמע.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
phrases.notes: A second statement of רבי יהודה, now about the list.

phrases.english: Between 'VaYomer' and 'Emet VeYatziv', one may not interrupt.
phrases.notes: Removes break 5 from the list. It is a no-interruption zone.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בֵּין ״וַיֹּאמֶר״ לֶ״אֱמֶת וְיַצִּיב״ — לֹא יַפְסִיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the fifth item in the list of בין הפרקים from step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, there is no interrupting at all between ויאמר and אמת ויציב.

steps.title: Why the paragraph of שמע comes before והיה אם שמוע
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה explains that שמע is said before והיה אם שמוע. One first accepts עול מלכות שמים, and only afterward accepts עול מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן קרחה said: Why does the paragraph of שמע come before והיה אם שמוע? So that a person first accepts upon himself the yoke of Heaven's kingship, and only after that accepts upon himself the yoke of the commandments.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a new question: why do we say the paragraphs of שמע in this order? In the תורה they are not next to each other. רבי יהושע בן קרחה answers for the first two paragraphs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first paragraph, שמע, is about accepting הקב"ה as King and believing in His oneness. The second paragraph, והיה אם שמוע, is about keeping the מצוות. Logically you must first accept the King before you can accept His commands, so the order of the paragraphs follows that logic.

keyTerms.meaning: The yoke of Heaven's kingship: accepting God as King
The yoke of the commandments: accepting the duty to keep the מצוות
Came first / preceded
A paragraph or section of the תורה

steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches a basic principle of עבודת ה': accepting God's authority is the foundation that comes before keeping the details of the מצוות.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha said:
Why did the paragraph of 'Shema' come first
before 'VeHaya im Shamoa'?
So that he will accept upon himself
the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven first,
phrases.notes: The paragraph of שמע declares God's oneness and our love for Him.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַחַר כָּךְ מְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל מִצְוֹת.
phrases.english: and afterward accept upon himself the yoke of the commandments.
phrases.notes: והיה אם שמוע speaks about keeping the מצוות and their reward and punishment.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה: לָמָּה קָדְמָה פָּרָשַׁת ״שְׁמַע״ לְ״וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמוֹעַ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה, moving from the laws of interrupting to the reason for the order of the paragraphs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמע precedes והיה אם שמוע because accepting עול מלכות שמים must come before accepting עול מצוות.

steps.title: Why והיה אם שמוע comes before ויאמר
steps.stepSummary: והיה אם שמוע comes before ויאמר because it applies by day and by night. ויאמר, the paragraph of ציצית, applies only by day.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why does והיה אם שמוע come before ויאמר? Because והיה אם שמוע applies both by day and by night, while ויאמר applies only by day.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן קרחה finishes his explanation. He explains why the second paragraph comes before the third.
steps.deeperAnalysis: והיה אם שמוע contains מצוות that apply at all times, such as learning תורה and מזוזה. ויאמר is about ציצית, and that מצוה applies only in the daytime. A paragraph whose content applies all the time takes precedence over one that applies only part of the time.

keyTerms.meaning: Applies / is in effect
Both by day and by night
The third paragraph of שמע, about ציצית

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean we skip ויאמר at night. It is still said. The point is only that its content, ציצית, is a daytime מצוה, so it is placed last.
steps.whatToRemember: The order is: שמע (accepting God), then והיה אם שמוע (accepting מצוות that apply day and night), then ויאמר (ציצית, a daytime-only מצוה).

phrases.english: And why does 'VeHaya im Shamoa' come before 'VaYomer'?
Because 'VeHaya im Shamoa' applies
both by day and by night,
while 'VaYomer' does not apply
except by day alone.
phrases.notes: ציצית is a daytime מצוה, as the verse says 'וראיתם אותו': you shall see it.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמוֹעַ״ לְ״וַיֹּאמֶר״ — שֶׁ״וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמוֹעַ״ נוֹהֵג בֵּין בַּיּוֹם וּבֵין בַּלַּיְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי יהושע בן קרחה's explanation of the order of the paragraphs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: והיה אם שמוע precedes ויאמר because it applies day and night, whereas ויאמר (ציצית) applies only by day.

steps.title: The גמרא tries to prove that מצוות צריכות כוונה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens and tries to prove from the משנה's words 'אם כוון לבו' that מצוות צריכות כוונה.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Learn from this that מצוות require intent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins. It looks back at the opening משנה (step 19), which said one fulfills the obligation only 'if he focused his heart.' From there it tries to prove a big general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person in the משנה is already saying the exact words of שמע. Yet the משנה still requires 'כוונה.' So the גמרא assumes this must mean intent to fulfill the מצוה. That would prove that without such intent, a מצוה does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmudic discussion that analyzes the משנה
Learn from this / we can conclude from it
מצוות require intent to fulfill the commandment

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether מצוות צריכות כוונה is a major question that comes up many times in ש"ס and has real practical halachic results.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Learn from this
that מצוות require intent.
phrases.notes: Based on the משנה's phrase 'אם כוון לבו יצא': if he focused his heart, he fulfilled his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the opening line of the משנה (step 19) to draw a general principle.
steps.raayaObject: The principle that מצוות צריכות כוונה
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's requirement 'אם כוון לבו יצא' for someone reading the שמע passage in the תורה

steps.title: Maybe the required intent is only intent to read
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Perhaps 'אם כוון לבו' only means intending to read the words, not intending to fulfill the מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'if he focused his heart' mean? Intent to read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof it just made. It suggests a different meaning for the משנה's words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'כוונה' here means only intent to read, the משנה tells us nothing about intent to fulfill a מצוה. Then the proof that מצוות צריכות כוונה falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: If he focused his heart (had intent)
To read

phrases.english: What is the meaning of 'if he focused his heart'?
To read.
phrases.notes: Intent to read the words, not intent to fulfill the מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 26 by reinterpreting the משנה's wording.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that מצוות צריכות כוונה from this משנה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed 'כוונה' means intent for the מצוה, but it could simply mean intent to read.

steps.title: But he is already reading
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rejection. How can the כוונה mean intent to read, when the person is already reading?
steps.simpleTranslation: Intent to read?! But he is reading!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from the last step. It argues that 'intent to read' makes no sense here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's case is a person who is actively reading the שמע passage in the תורה. Requiring him to 'intend to read' seems pointless, because reading is exactly what he is doing. So the כוונה must be something more, meaning intent for the מצוה, which would bring back the original proof.

keyTerms.meaning: But he is reading!

phrases.english: To read?!
But he is already reading!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reinterpretation offered in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'אם כוון לבו' means intent to read
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case is someone already reading the words, so requiring intent to read would be meaningless.

steps.title: He is reading to correct the text
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is someone reading in order to proofread the text. Such a person needs intent to actually read the words.
steps.simpleTranslation: It refers to one who is reading in order to correct the text.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the idea that 'כוונה' means intent to read. It explains what kind of reading the משנה is talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person checking a ספר תורה for mistakes looks at the letters and spelling and is not really 'reading' the words as speech. So the משנה teaches that he fulfills his obligation only if he intends to actually read the words. Since this is all the משנה requires, it does not prove that מצוות צריכות כוונה.

keyTerms.meaning: To proofread / correct errors in the text
One who reads

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא concluded that מצוות do not need כוונה. It only showed that this משנה is no proof either way.
steps.whatToRemember: The proof from 'אם כוון לבו' fails: the כוונה may only be intent to read, for someone who was reading to proofread. The question of מצוות צריכות כוונה stays open here.

phrases.english: It refers to one who reads in order to correct the text.
phrases.notes: He is checking spelling, so he needs intent to actually read the words aloud as reading.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 28 and so upholds the דחיה of step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to a specific type of reader
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the person is reading the words, 'כוונה' must mean intent to fulfill the מצוה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The person was reading to proofread, so 'כוונה' means intent to actually read. The משנה does not prove that מצוות צריכות כוונה.

steps.title: A ברייתא: in which language may קריאת שמע be said?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records a dispute. רבי says קריאת שמע must be said as written, in לשון הקודש. The חכמים say any language is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: קריאת שמע must be said as it is written. These are the words of רבי. The חכמים say: it may be said in any language.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a ברייתא. Two opinions argue about whether קריאת שמע may be said in a language other than לשון הקודש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי holds that the exact original words, in their original language, are required. The חכמים hold that the language is not essential. This dispute sets up the next steps, where the גמרא looks for each side's source.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught. This opens a ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself.
As it is written, meaning in its original Hebrew wording.
The words of רבי, meaning רבי יהודה הנשיא.
In any language.

steps.confusionAlert: When the גמרא says just "רבי" with no name, it means רבי יהודה הנשיא, the one who compiled the משנה. It is not a general word for "a rabbi."

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Shema must be recited as it is written,
these are the words of Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi).
phrases.notes: A two-word row, because it is a complete attribution.

phrases.english: And the Sages say: in any language.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע כִּכְתָבָהּ, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא and a new topic, the language of קריאת שמע. It will later connect to the larger discussion of כוונה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי: קריאת שמע only in its original wording. חכמים: in any language.

steps.title: What is רבי's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבי's opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי learns that קריאת שמע must be said in its original language. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a request for information, not an attack. The גמרא wants to know which פסוק supports רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason? It asks for the source or logic behind an opinion.

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the first opinion in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק teaches that קריאת שמע must be said in its original language.

steps.title: רבי learns from the word ״וְהָיוּ״
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says ״וְהָיוּ״, "and they shall be." רבי reads this as: the words must stay as they are.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says "וְהָיוּ", "they shall be." This means: as they are, so shall they be.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי's source. The word ״וְהָיוּ״ teaches that the words of שמע must stay unchanged.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי reads ״וְהָיוּ״ as "they shall stay in their original form." Translating them would change their form, so they must be said in לשון הקודש.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק says. It introduces a source from the Torah.
And they shall be (דברים ו:ו).
As they are, so shall they be. In other words, unchanged.

phrases.english: The verse says: "And they shall be"
as they are, so shall they be.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about רבי's source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word ״וְהָיוּ״ teaches that the words must stay in their original form.

steps.title: What is the חכמים's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now asks for the reason behind the חכמים's opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים, what is their reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where the חכמים learn that any language is allowed. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the other side of the ברייתא also needs a source. The question follows the same pattern as the question about רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: Their reason (plural, referring to the חכמים).
The Rabbis. Here it refers to the חכמים of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, what is their reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same kind of question as step 31, now about the second opinion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק allows saying קריאת שמע in any language.

steps.title: The חכמים learn from the word ״שְׁמַע״
steps.stepSummary: The word ״שְׁמַע״ means "hear" in the sense of understanding. So any language you understand is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says "שְׁמַע", "hear." This means: in any language that you hear, that is, understand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the חכמים's source. ״שְׁמַע״ means you must understand the words, so any language you understand works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the חכמים, the main point of ״שְׁמַע״ is understanding, not the exact sounds of the Hebrew. So any language you understand is acceptable.

keyTerms.meaning: Hear. Here it is read as "understand."
Hear, meaning understand.

steps.confusionAlert: Here ״שְׁמַע״ does not mean only hearing with the ears. It means understanding.

phrases.english: The verse says: "Hear" —
in any language that you hear (understand).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא: ״שְׁמַע״ — בְּכָל לָשׁוֹן שֶׁאַתָּה שׁוֹמֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the חכמים's source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״שְׁמַע״ means understand, so any language you understand is valid.

steps.title: What does רבי do with the word ״שְׁמַע״?
steps.stepSummary: The word ״שְׁמַע״ is in רבי's Torah too. Why doesn't he learn from it that any language is allowed?
steps.simpleTranslation: And for רבי too, isn't it written "שְׁמַע"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי. The same word the חכמים use is also in the פסוק for him, so how does he explain it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If ״שְׁמַע״ teaches "any language," רבי's view seems to contradict the פסוק. רבי must have a different use for this word.

keyTerms.meaning: Also, too.
But it is written! This introduces a challenge from a פסוק.

phrases.english: And for Rabbi too,
isn't it written "Hear"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the חכמים's source from step 34 to challenge רבי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's opinion that קריאת שמע must be said only in its original wording.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word ״שְׁמַע״, which seems to allow any language, is written in the פסוק that רבי also accepts.

steps.title: רבי uses ״שְׁמַע״ for saying it out loud
steps.stepSummary: רבי needs ״שְׁמַע״ for a different rule: say the words loud enough that your ears hear what your mouth says.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs that word to teach: let your ears hear what you bring out from your mouth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי. The word ״שְׁמַע״ is already used for another rule, so it cannot also teach "any language."
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי reads ״שְׁמַע״ as "hear" in the literal sense, with the ears. So it teaches that קריאת שמע must be said out loud. Since the word is "busy" with this rule, it is not available to allow other languages.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it (for something else). The פסוק is already used to teach a different rule.
Let your ears hear.
What you say with your mouth.

steps.whatToRemember: רבי: ״וְהָיוּ״ means the original language only, and ״שְׁמַע״ means say it out loud. חכמים: ״שְׁמַע״ means any language you understand.
steps.whyThisMatters: This creates the rule of הַשְׁמָעָה לְאָזְנַיִם, saying קריאת שמע loud enough to hear yourself. The גמרא will soon discuss this rule.

phrases.english: He needs that (verse) for:
Make your ears hear
what you bring out from your mouth.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהוּא מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ: הַשְׁמַע לְאָזְנֶיךָ מַה שֶּׁאַתָּה מוֹצִיא מִפִּיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The פסוק is used for a different teaching (מיבעי ליה).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ״שְׁמַע״ seemed to teach that any language is allowed, which would contradict רבי.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי, ״שְׁמַע״ teaches that you must say קריאת שמע loud enough for your own ears to hear.

steps.title: What do the Sages do about hearing your own words?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the רבנן deal with the rule that you must hear yourself say שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Rabbis?
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן already used ״שְׁמַע״ to allow any language. So the גמרא asks: where do they learn that you must hear the words you say?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 36, רבי used ״שְׁמַע״ to teach that your ears must hear your mouth. The רבנן have already used that word for the language rule. So the גמרא wants to know what they hold about hearing yourself.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, the majority opinion arguing with רבי

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
phrases.notes: A short question. It means: how do the Rabbis handle the hearing rule?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the previous answer about רבי back onto the רבנן
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the רבנן hold about hearing your own recitation, since they used ״שְׁמַע״ for language

steps.title: The Sages hold you are יוצא even without hearing yourself
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן follow the view that someone who did not hear his own words is still יצא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They hold like the one who said: if he did not let his ears hear, he has still fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן do not need a source for the hearing rule. They hold that if you said שמע too quietly to hear yourself, you are still יצא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן do not need ״שְׁמַע״ for a hearing rule, because for them hearing yourself is not required. So they are free to use the word for the language rule. Both opinions now fit their sources.

keyTerms.meaning: Said it loud enough for his own ears to hear
He has fulfilled his obligation
Like the one who said (following an opinion stated elsewhere)

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the רבנן say you should speak quietly. It only means that after the fact you are still יצא if you did not hear yourself.

phrases.english: They hold like the one who said:
If he did not let his ears hear, he has fulfilled his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 37
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן do not need a source, since they hold hearing yourself is not required

steps.title: What do the Sages do with ״וְהָיוּ״?
steps.stepSummary: The word ״וְהָיוּ״ is in the רבנן's Torah too. What do they learn from it?
steps.simpleTranslation: And for the Rabbis too, isn't it written ״וְהָיוּ״?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the רבנן. רבי used ״וְהָיוּ״ to require the original language, so what do the רבנן do with this word?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the mirror image of Step 35. There the גמרא asked what רבי does with ״שְׁמַע״. Now it asks what the רבנן do with ״וְהָיוּ״, since every word in the פסוק should teach something.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is written!
Also, too

phrases.english: And according to the Rabbis too,
isn't it written "and they shall be"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors the challenge of Step 35, now aimed at the רבנן
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's opinion that any language is allowed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ״וְהָיוּ״ seems to teach that the words must stay as written. If the רבנן ignore it, the word teaches them nothing.

steps.title: The Sages use ״וְהָיוּ״ to forbid saying it out of order
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn from ״וְהָיוּ״ that you may not say שמע out of order.
steps.simpleTranslation: They need that word to teach that one may not read it out of order.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן do use ״וְהָיוּ״. For them it means the words must stay in their order, not that they must stay in their language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides read ״וְהָיוּ״ as "keep it as it is." רבי applies that to language. The רבנן apply it to the order of the words, so you cannot start from the end.

keyTerms.meaning: They need it (for another teaching)
Backwards, out of order

phrases.english: They need that one
to teach that one may not read it out of order.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 39
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the פסוק to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן have no use for ״וְהָיוּ״
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן use ״וְהָיוּ״ to forbid reading out of order

steps.title: Where does רבי learn the order rule?
steps.stepSummary: רבי used ״וְהָיוּ״ for language, so where does he learn that you may not read out of order?
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי, from where does he learn that one may not read out of order?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for רבי's source for the order rule. He already used ״וְהָיוּ״ for language, so he needs a different source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees you may not say שמע out of order. The רבנן just got that rule from ״וְהָיוּ״. Since רבי used that word for language, the גמרא asks where he gets it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he learn it?

phrases.english: And רבי, that one may not read out of order,
from where does he learn it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי, שֶׁלֹּא יִקְרָא לְמַפְרֵעַ מְנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from Step 40: the order rule needs a source in רבי's opinion too
steps.sheelahInformationSought: רבי's source for not reading שמע out of order

steps.title: רבי learns the order rule from ״הַדְּבָרִים״
steps.stepSummary: רבי learns the order rule from the extra ה in ״הַדְּבָרִים״. The רבנן do not learn anything from that ה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from ״דְּבָרִים״ versus ״הַדְּבָרִים״. And the Rabbis do not learn anything from ״דְּבָרִים״ versus ״הַדְּבָרִים״.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי learns the order rule from the extra ה in ״הַדְּבָרִים״. The גמרא then adds that the רבנן do not learn from that ה, which is why they need ״וְהָיוּ״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have said "words" (״דְּבָרִים״). Instead it says "THE words" (״הַדְּבָרִים״), meaning these exact words in their set order. רבי learns from this extra letter, and the רבנן do not, so each side ends up with a source for every rule.

keyTerms.meaning: He learns it from
"The words", with the extra ה meaning "the"
They do not learn anything from it

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree on the order rule and both use ״וְהָיוּ״. רבי uses it for language and gets the order rule from ״הַדְּבָרִים״. The רבנן use it for order and get the language rule from ״שְׁמַע״.

phrases.english: He learns it from "words" versus "the words."
phrases.notes: The extra ה ("the") points to these specific words in their set order.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis do not learn anything from "words" versus "the words."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 41 and explains why the רבנן cannot use the same source
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי learns the order rule from the extra ה in ״הַדְּבָרִים״; the רבנן do not learn from it

steps.title: Does רבי hold the whole Torah may be read in any language?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רבי must hold the rest of the Torah may be read in any language. Otherwise, why would ״וְהָיוּ״ be needed just for שמע?
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean רבי holds the entire Torah may be said in any language? Because if you think it may only be said in לשון הקודש, why did the Torah need to write ״וְהָיוּ״?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a possible conclusion from רבי's opinion. It is setting up the next move, and the answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every part of the Torah already had to be in לשון הקודש, there would be no need for a special word saying שמע must be in Hebrew. So the fact that רבי needs ״וְהָיוּ״ for שמע seems to show that, for him, the rest of the Torah may be read in any language. The word ״לְמֵימְרָא״ ("Is that to say?") often means the גמרא may later reject this conclusion.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (introduces a possible conclusion)
In any language
The holy language, Hebrew
If you were to think
The Merciful One (refers to God / the Torah)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the final answer. ״לְמֵימְרָא״ is the גמרא trying out a conclusion, and it may be pushed back in the next lines.

phrases.english: Is that to say that Rabbi holds
that the entire Torah
may be said in any language?
For if you were to think
that it may only be said in the holy language,
why would I need the ״וְהָיוּ״ that the Torah wrote?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the sources of the argument to what רבי's opinion means for the rest of the Torah
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבי's need for ״וְהָיוּ״ shows that he allows the rest of the Torah in any language

steps.title: רבי needs ״וְהָיוּ״ because ״שְׁמַע״ is written
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion that רבי holds the whole Torah may be read in any language. ״וְהָיוּ״ is needed for שמע anyway, because the word ״שְׁמַע״ could have led us to permit any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was necessary because ״שְׁמַע״ is written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 43. רבי needed ״וְהָיוּ״ even if the rest of the Torah may only be read in Hebrew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ״שְׁמַע״ ("hear, understand") could suggest that שמע may be said in any language you understand, which is how the רבנן read it. Without ״וְהָיוּ״ we would have followed that reading. So רבי needs ״וְהָיוּ״ to block it, and we cannot conclude anything about the rest of the Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: It was necessary (the verse is not extra)
Because it is written
Hear / understand. The רבנן read it as permission to use any language you understand

phrases.english: It was necessary, because "Hear" is written.
phrases.notes: Without "and they shall be" we would have learned from "Hear" that any language is fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference proposed in step 43
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that רבי allows the rest of the Torah in any language
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed ״וְהָיוּ״ would be extra if the rest of the Torah had to be in Hebrew. In fact it is needed to counter ״שְׁמַע״.

steps.title: Do the רבנן hold the whole Torah must be in Hebrew?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the mirror-image proof. It suggests the רבנן must hold that the rest of the Torah may only be read in לשון הקודש. Otherwise, why would they need ״שְׁמַע״ to permit any language for שמע?
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean the רבנן hold that the whole Torah may only be said in the holy language? If you thought it may be said in any language, why would I need the word ״שְׁמַע״ that the Torah wrote?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks the same kind of question about the רבנן. It suggests that their use of ״שְׁמַע״ shows they hold the rest of the Torah must be read in Hebrew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic is this. If every part of the Torah could already be read in any language, there would be no need for a special word to permit it for שמע. So the רבנן's use of ״שְׁמַע״ would seem to prove that the default for the Torah is Hebrew only.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say? (introduces a suggested inference)
The holy language, Hebrew
For if it would enter your mind
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
Why do I need it?

phrases.english: Is this to say that the Rabbis hold
that the entire Torah, all of it,
may only be said in the holy language?
For if it would enter your mind
that it may be said in any language,
why do I need "Hear", which the Torah wrote?!
phrases.notes: The word would seem to be extra.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel to step 43, now applied to the רבנן instead of רבי
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the רבנן's need for ״שְׁמַע״ shows they hold the rest of the Torah must be read in Hebrew

steps.title: The רבנן need ״שְׁמַע״ because ״וְהָיוּ״ is written
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof about the רבנן. ״שְׁמַע״ is needed anyway, because ״וְהָיוּ״ could have led us to require Hebrew for שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was necessary because ״וְהָיוּ״ is written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 45, using the mirror image of its answer in step 44.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ״וְהָיוּ״ ("and they shall be" as they are) could suggest that שמע must stay in its original language, as רבי reads it. The רבנן need ״שְׁמַע״ to teach that any language is fine for שמע. So we learn nothing about the rest of the Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: And they shall be. רבי reads it as "they must stay as they are," meaning in Hebrew

steps.whatToRemember: Both words are needed. ״שְׁמַע״ and ״וְהָיוּ״ each push in opposite directions. Each side needs its own word to override the other word. So neither side's reading proves anything about how the rest of the Torah may be read.

phrases.english: It was necessary, because "and they shall be" is written.
phrases.notes: Without "Hear" we would have learned from "and they shall be" that שמע must be in Hebrew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference proposed in step 45
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that the רבנן require Hebrew for the rest of the Torah
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed ״שְׁמַע״ would be extra. In fact it is needed to counter ״וְהָיוּ״.

steps.title: A ברייתא: שמע may not be said out of order
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that opens a new section. ״וְהָיוּ״ teaches that one may not say שמע out of order.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: ״וְהָיוּ״ teaches that one may not read it out of order.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the language debate and quotes a ברייתא. It begins with the rule we already saw in step 40, that שמע must be said in order.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״וְהָיוּ״ means the words must be "as they are," in their written order. This opens a ברייתא that goes on to discuss how much of שמע needs כוונה.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught (introduces a ברייתא)
Out of order, backwards

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"And they shall be" teaches that one may not read it out of order.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא. It echoes the order rule from step 40.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמע may not be said out of order (learned from ״וְהָיוּ״).

steps.title: How much of שמע needs כוונה, according to רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns from ״עַל לְבָבֶךָ״ that שמע needs כוונה. It asks whether the whole פרשה needs it. Then it uses ״הָאֵלֶּה״ to limit the requirement to the first part. This is the view of רבי אליעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: ״הַדְּבָרִים … עַל לְבָבֶךָ״ teaches that שמע needs focused intention. You might think the whole paragraph needs intention. So the verse says ״הָאֵלֶּה״ ("these"). Up to here you need intention. From here on you do not. These are the words of רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues. It sets up a possible mistake, that the whole paragraph needs כוונה, and then corrects it with the word ״הָאֵלֶּה״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "On your heart" shows that the words need focus. ״הָאֵלֶּה״ ("these") narrows it to these specific words, the first part only (רש"י: until "עַל לְבָבֶךָ"). After that point, you still fulfill the מצוה even without כוונה.

keyTerms.meaning: Focused intention while reciting
I might have thought (introduces a wrong assumption)
Therefore the verse says (introduces the correcting word)
These. A limiting word: only these words
The תנא who holds this view

steps.confusionAlert: ״עַד כָּאן... מִכָּאן וְאֵילָךְ״ does not mean the rest of שמע may be skipped. It must still be said. Only the requirement of focused כוונה is limited to the first part.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the halacha that the first part of שמע requires special כוונה. The גמרא will go on to discuss other views about exactly where that part ends.

phrases.english: "The words... on your heart" teaches that intention is required.
I might have thought that the whole paragraph
requires intention?
Therefore the verse says "these."
Up to here, intention is required;
from here on, intention is not required.
These are the words of Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל תְּהֵא כָּל הַפָּרָשָׁה צְרִיכָה כַּוָּונָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא. It moves from the rule of order to the rule of כוונה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי אליעזר, only the first part of שמע (until ״עַל לְבָבֶךָ״) requires כוונה.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא begins to challenge רבי אליעזר with a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא responds to רבי אליעזר and announces that he is about to quote a פסוק that argues against limiting כוונה to the first part of שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to him: But the פסוק says:
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא starts to answer רבי אליעזר. This line is a setup, and the actual פסוק he quotes comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר limited the need for כוונה to the first section. The words ״הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר״ signal that רבי עקיבא is about to bring a פסוק that points the other way. He will argue that the requirement covers more than רבי אליעזר allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא who disagrees with רבי אליעזר in this ברייתא
"He said to him." This marks a direct reply to the previous speaker.
"But it says." This formula introduces a pasuk brought as a counter-proof.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not stop here thinking רבי עקיבא's argument is finished. This line only introduces his proof. The פסוק he relies on comes next.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said to him:
phrases.notes: "Him" refers to רבי אליעזר, whose view was just stated.

phrases.english: But the verse states:
phrases.notes: This sets up a פסוק that will be used against רבי אליעזר's limitation.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a direct response to רבי אליעזר's derivation from ״הָאֵלֶּה״ in step 48.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר's claim that כוונה is only needed for the first part of שמע.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק, still to be quoted, will show that the requirement of כוונה reaches further than רבי אליעזר limited it.
